chapter: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
title: Why you couldn't follow Monk: closing his ears
summary: Monk played against the meter; Simmons listened to Milt Jackson instead.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: Back to New York. You were just going to the Royal Roost with Monk. Right?
Then we digressed into bop. Weren't you about to say something about Monk? About working with Monk.

Yes. Well, working with Monk, you couldn't follow him. He played between the keys, he played against the meter, and he would just play all over the piano, you know. It wasn't anything you could follow. If you didn't know the tune, you couldn't play with him. Now, if you're playing by ear, you had to listen to a melodic line. So I

trained my ears to listening to Bags, you know, Milt Jackson. I'd just throw Monk out of my ear. I just closed my ears to him completely. Of course Chuck Parham had told me years ago, in the early '30s, "Man, close your ears." I said, "Man, how do you close your ears?" He said, "Just don't hear it." I couldn't understand that at that time. But I grew up to be a big boy and found out how to close my ears.
Uh-huh. So you closed your ears to Monk, then.
